chapterTitle: The Weak and the Strong — Whose Servant Is He?
themeTitle: “To His Own Lord He Stands or Falls” — When Being Right Is Not the Same as Walking in Love

scripture.text: Now accept one who is weak in faith, but not for disputes over opinions.
scripture.understanding: The chapter opens with a command aimed at the strong, not the weak: receive him. Proslambano is warm, personal welcome — the word for taking a man to yourself, into your house and to your table, not merely tolerating that he exists in the room. Then Paul builds a fence around the welcome: receive him, but not so you can put his opinions on trial. Do not welcome a brother in order to work on him.

scripture.text: One man has faith to eat all things, but he who is weak eats only vegetables.
scripture.understanding: Paul defines the dispute with deliberate plainness — it is about dinner. A Jewish believer in Rome, with no reliable kosher slaughter and a meat market whose supply ran through pagan temples, often solved the problem the way Daniel did in Babylon: vegetables only. Notice Paul never says the weak man is less devout; frequently he is the more careful man. He is weak in faith in one precise sense — his faith has not yet taken hold of how far Christ has actually freed him.

scripture.text: Don’t let him who eats despise him who doesn’t eat. Don’t let him who doesn’t eat judge him who eats, for God has accepted him.
scripture.understanding: Two different sins are sitting at one table. The strong man's sin is contempt — exoutheneo, to count a person as nothing, to write him off with a smirk. The weak man's sin is condemnation — krino, to hand down a verdict. Paul cuts both down with one fact: God has accepted him. If God has already received the man, your rejection of him is not a higher standard; it is a contradiction of God.

scripture.text: Who are you who judge another’s servant? To his own lord he stands or falls. Yes, he will be made to stand, for God has power to make him stand.
scripture.understanding: The question is blunt and it is meant to sting: you are correcting somebody else's household slave. An oiketes answers to the master who owns him, in the house where he lives — and you do not live there. Then Paul adds the sentence that dismantles your anxiety about the man: he will be made to stand. Not because his convictions are correct, but because God has the power to hold him up.

scripture.text: One man esteems one day as more important. Another esteems every day alike. Let each man be fully assured in his own mind.
scripture.understanding: The second disputed area is the calendar — Sabbaths, feast days, fast days. Paul refuses to legislate, and instead demands something far harder than compliance: personal conviction. Plerophoreo means to be carried to full measure, entirely convinced. God is not after your conformity to the loudest personality in the room; He is after settled faith in your own mind.

scripture.text: He who observes the day, observes it to the Lord; and he who does not observe the day, to the Lord he does not observe it. He who eats, eats to the Lord, for he gives God thanks. He who doesn’t eat, to the Lord he doesn’t eat, and gives God thanks.
scripture.understanding: Here is the sentence that should end most of your arguments: both men are doing it to the Lord, and both are giving God thanks. The man with the empty plate and the man with the full one are facing the same direction. When you can hear a brother genuinely thank God over a choice you would never make, you have just met the real issue — his Master, not his menu.

scripture.text: For none of us lives to himself, and none dies to himself.
scripture.understanding: Paul lifts the discussion off the dinner table and into eternity. No believer is a private citizen; there is no such thing as a life lived to yourself, and even your dying is not your own private event. This cuts in both directions in this chapter: it demolishes the isolation of 'it is nobody's business but mine,' and it demolishes your claim to run somebody else's life.

scripture.text: For if we live, we live to the Lord. Or if we die, we die to the Lord. If therefore we live or die, we are the Lord’s.
scripture.understanding: The word that settles everything is not 'mine' but 'the Lord's.' Living or dying, the believer's address never changes: he belongs to Jesus. That is the answer about the man you have been judging — he is not yours to own, he is already owned — and it is the floor under your own fear of dying. Whichever side of death you are on, you are on the Lord's side of it.

scripture.text: For to this end Christ died, rose, and lived again, that he might be Lord of both the dead and the living.
scripture.understanding: Paul grounds a squabble about food in the cross and the empty tomb. Christ did not die merely to forgive you; He died, rose, and lived again in order to hold lordship over the dead and the living. So every time you climb into the judge's seat over a brother, you are reaching for territory that Jesus bought with His own blood.

scripture.text: But you, why do you judge your brother? Or you again, why do you despise your brother? For we will all stand before the judgment seat of Christ.
scripture.understanding: Twice in one verse Paul says 'your brother' — the person in your crosshairs is family. Then he puts a picture in front of you: the bema, the raised judgment platform of a Roman city, the very kind of platform Paul himself had been dragged before in Corinth, the city he is writing from. There is a seat, it is occupied, and it is not yours.

scripture.text:
For it is written,
“‘As I live,’ says the Lord, ‘to me every knee will bow.
Every tongue will confess to God.’”
scripture.understanding: Paul reaches for Isaiah 45:23 — the passage where the LORD swears by Himself that no other god will ever receive worship — and drops it into an argument about food, fused with the old oath formula 'as I live, says the LORD.' Read it as the courtroom scene it is: at that seat no knee stays locked and no tongue stays silent. Every believer who ever irritated you will be on his knees worshiping — and so will you, beside him.

scripture.text: So then each one of us will give account of himself to God.
scripture.understanding: The decisive word is himself. You will not be asked to explain your brother, and he will not be asked to explain you. If the account you give is entirely your own, then the file you have been quietly keeping on somebody else is not evidence for your case — it is a distraction from your own hearing.

scripture.text: Therefore let’s not judge one another any more, but judge this rather, that no man put a stumbling block in his brother’s way, or an occasion for falling.
scripture.understanding: Paul does not abolish judgment here; he redirects it. Stop passing verdicts on people and start passing a verdict on your own behavior. A proskomma is a stone left lying where a man will strike his foot in the dark; a skandalon is the trigger-stick of a trap. Make the decision once, and let it stand for life: nothing of mine goes in a brother's road.

scripture.text: I know, and am persuaded in the Lord Jesus, that nothing is unclean of itself; except that to him who considers anything to be unclean, to him it is unclean.
scripture.understanding: Paul takes a side, and it must be said plainly — the strong are right. Nothing is koinon, common or defiling, in itself, and he says he knows this 'in the Lord Jesus,' almost certainly leaning on Jesus' own ruling that declared all foods clean (Mark 7:19). But the second half of the verse binds the first: what a man believes about it holds him. Truth does not become false when a conscience disagrees — yet no man may act out past his own conscience.

scripture.text: Yet if because of food your brother is grieved, you walk no longer in love. Don’t destroy with your food him for whom Christ died.
scripture.understanding: Now the knife goes in. You are not told you are wrong about food; you are told you have stopped walking in love — and love is the fulfillment of the law (13:10). Then comes the sentence that should stop you cold: the man being wounded by your dinner is a man Christ died for. Weigh the two things honestly against each other — your plate, and His blood.

scripture.text: Then don’t let your good be slandered,
scripture.understanding: Your liberty really is a good thing; Paul never once calls it otherwise. But a good thing used without love earns a bad name, and the reputation you damage is never only your own. Freedom that leaves casualties behind it will be spoken of as evil — and the grace that gave you the freedom takes the slander with you.

scripture.text: for God’s Kingdom is not eating and drinking, but righteousness, peace, and joy in the Holy Spirit.
scripture.understanding: Here is the measuring stick for every disputed thing you have ever argued about: the Kingdom of God is not built out of menus. It is righteousness, peace, and joy in the Holy Spirit. So test your convictions by all three — if a position of yours produces righteousness while wrecking peace and killing joy, you are holding kingdom vocabulary without kingdom substance.

scripture.text: For he who serves Christ in these things is acceptable to God and approved by men.
scripture.understanding: Serve Christ in these three things and two results follow: God is pleased, and watching people can actually see it. Notice what draws the approval of onlookers — not your liberty and not your scruples, but a life of righteousness that keeps the peace. No one has ever been argued into the Kingdom by our food fights.

scripture.text: So then, let us follow after things which make for peace, and things by which we may build one another up.
scripture.understanding: Peace here is not a mood you wait for; it is prey you hunt — dioko, to pursue, to chase down. And the second pursuit is oikodome, construction work: the deliberate building up of another person. Hold every conversation you are about to have up against those two words. Is this pursuing peace? Is this construction?

scripture.text: Don’t overthrow God’s work for food’s sake. All things indeed are clean, however it is evil for that man who creates a stumbling block by eating.
scripture.understanding: Kataluo is the demolition word — to pull a building down stone by stone, the word Jesus used of the temple being thrown down. Paul has just told you to build (v. 19); now he names the opposite: for the sake of a meal, you can begin dismantling what God is constructing in a person. He repeats that all things are clean — the truth has not moved — and then calls being right without love by its proper name: evil.

scripture.text: It is good to not eat meat, drink wine, nor do anything by which your brother stumbles, is offended, or is made weak.
scripture.understanding: This is not a permanent rule against meat and wine; it is a good — kalon, beautiful, fitting — that love chooses in a particular place, for a particular brother. And notice how far the sentence reaches past the dinner table: 'nor do anything.' Food was never the point. Food was only the case study for every liberty you own.

scripture.text: Do you have faith? Have it to yourself before God. Happy is he who doesn’t judge himself in that which he approves.
scripture.understanding: Your convictions are real, and their first home is the presence of God, not the middle of the room. Paul is not telling you to hide your faith; he is telling you not to weaponize it. Then he pronounces a blessing on the man who carries no self-accusation about what he permits himself — a clear conscience is one of the quietest joys God gives.

scripture.text: But he who doubts is condemned if he eats, because it isn’t of faith; and whatever is not of faith is sin.
scripture.understanding: The man who eats while still uncertain stands self-condemned — not because the food was dirty, but because he acted against his own conviction of God's will. Then Paul writes the principle that reaches into every corner of a life: whatever is not of faith is sin. Anything you cannot do in settled confidence that God approves it is sin for you, even when the thing itself is perfectly clean.

scripture.text: Now to him who is able to establish you according to my Good News and the preaching of Jesus Christ, according to the revelation of the mystery which has been kept secret through long ages,
scripture.understanding: In most Bibles you will ever open, this doxology is printed as Romans 16:25-27; the manuscript tradition behind this translation places it right here, at the end of chapter 14. Do not let the numbering distract you — watch how precisely it lands on the argument: the God who has power to make your weak brother stand (v. 4) is the God who is able to establish you. Sterizo means to set a thing fast so it cannot be shifted. The same gospel that saved you is the gospel that steadies you — and it is His work, not your correctness, that holds anyone upright.

scripture.text: but now is revealed, and by the Scriptures of the prophets, according to the commandment of the eternal God, is made known for obedience of faith to all the nations;
scripture.understanding: The mystery hidden through long ages is now published openly, and the stated goal is 'obedience of faith to all the nations' — the very phrase Paul opened the letter with, where he received apostleship 'for obedience of faith among all the nations' (1:5). The bookends match. And look at the target: all the nations. The very Jew-and-Gentile mixture that has been arguing over dinner in Rome is not an accident of the church; it is the point of the entire plan.

scripture.text: to the only wise God, through Jesus Christ, to whom be the glory forever! Amen.
scripture.understanding: The letter's argument ends on its knees. There is only one wise God — which quietly settles the whole chapter, because that room in Rome was full of people who each believed they were the wise one. The glory goes to Him forever, through Jesus Christ: not to the strong for their knowledge, and not to the weak for their scruples.

visualMeditations.title: The Table With Two Plates
visualMeditations.image: A rented room above a Roman street. A borrowed table, a lamp, bread going round. On one side sits a Gentile believer with meat on his plate — bought that morning at the public meat market, where a great deal of the supply came off animals killed on pagan altars, and he thought nothing of it, because Christ has made him free. On the other side sits a Jewish believer, back in the city only a few years after Claudius threw every Jew out of Rome, and in front of him is a bowl of lentils and greens. He will not touch the meat; he cannot know whose altar it crossed. Nobody says a word. But two looks travel across that table — one of them a smirk, the other a sentence — and the room goes cold.
visualMeditations.meaning: Paul is not writing theory. He is writing to a congregation that had been torn in half by an imperial decree and stitched back together badly. The strong man's glance says, 'Still living in the shadows, are you?' The weak man's glance says, 'And you call yourself holy.' Two men, one Lord, one table — and both of them sinning with their eyes. Before you ever open your mouth about a disputed thing, God has already read the look on your face.

visualMeditations.title: Correcting Another Man's Servant
visualMeditations.image: Picture yourself walking into a house that is not yours. In the courtyard a household slave is working, and he is doing it wrong — wrong hour, wrong method, wrong everything by your standards. So you start giving orders. You raise your voice. You tell him what his duties really are. And then a door opens on the far side of the courtyard, and the master of that house steps out, and looks at you, and says one sentence: 'Who are you?' He is not asking your name. He is asking on what authority a stranger is disciplining his servant in his own courtyard.
visualMeditations.meaning: An oiketes was not a hired man; he was a member of the household, owned, fed, and answerable to one master alone. That is the picture Paul chooses for your brother in Christ. The believer you are itching to fix is not unsupervised — he is under management, and it is not yours. And then the mercy in the middle of the rebuke: he will be made to stand. The master in that courtyard is not only the one with the right to correct him; He is the one with the power to hold him up.

visualMeditations.title: The Bema at the End of the Argument
visualMeditations.image: In every Roman city there was a raised stone platform in the public square — the bema — where the magistrate sat and cases were decided in the open air. Paul is writing from Corinth, where he had himself been hauled in front of Gallio's bema by an angry crowd. Now he tells you to see one: the platform, the seat, the Judge. And here is the detail that will change how you argue this week — the brother you have been judging is not standing on trial in front of you. He is standing beside you, in the same crowd, waiting for the same hearing. And every knee in that square, his and yours, is already bending.
visualMeditations.meaning: There is a judgment seat, and it is not vacant, and you are not on it. Paul quotes Isaiah 45:23 — the fiercest monotheism in the Old Testament, where the LORD swears by Himself that every knee will bow to Him alone — and applies it to standing before Christ. The One you were trying to substitute for is God. And verse 12 removes your last excuse: each of us gives account of himself. Not of his brother. Of himself.

visualMeditations.title: Tearing Down a Building for a Plate of Food
visualMeditations.image: See two men on the same site. One is a builder — oikodome — carrying stone, setting it, raising a wall course by course. The other has a crowbar, and he is prising the stones out from underneath: kataluo, the demolition word, the word Jesus used for a temple being thrown down. Now look at what the demolition man is being paid. It is not treasure, not power, not even pleasure worth the name. It is a meal. He is dismantling something God is building in a human being for the sake of one dinner he did not have to eat.
visualMeditations.meaning: God is building a person over there — slowly, patiently, stone by stone. Your liberty is real and your theology may be flawless, and you can still be the man with the crowbar. That is why Paul calls it 'evil' in verse 20 without softening it: not the food, which is clean, but the wrecking. And note the price tag. Almost nobody trades away a brother for something magnificent. We trade him for a plate, a joke, a night out, the last word in an argument.

structure.label: Receive Him — God Already Has (v. 1-3)
structure.body: Welcome the weak in faith without putting his opinions on trial; the strong must stop despising, the weak must stop condemning, because God has accepted the man they are both mishandling.

structure.label: Whose Servant Is He? (v. 4-6)
structure.body: You are correcting another man's household slave; his own Lord will hold him up. On days as on food, each man must be fully convinced in his own mind — and both men are giving thanks to the same Lord.

structure.label: Lord of the Dead and the Living (v. 7-9)
structure.body: No believer lives or dies to himself; living or dying we are the Lord's, because Christ died, rose, and lived again precisely in order to be Lord of both.

structure.label: The Judgment Seat and the Account (v. 10-12)
structure.body: Judging and despising a brother are both attempts to occupy a seat that already has an occupant; every knee will bow, and each one will give account of himself.

structure.label: Judge This Instead (v. 13-15)
structure.body: Redirect your judging: decide once, for life, never to lay a stumbling block in a brother's road. Nothing is unclean of itself, but wounding him over food means you are no longer walking in love — and he is a man Christ died for.

structure.label: The Kingdom Is Not Eating and Drinking (v. 16-19)
structure.body: Don't let your liberty earn a bad name; the Kingdom is righteousness, peace, and joy in the Holy Spirit — so hunt down peace and build one another up.

structure.label: Do Not Demolish God's Work (v. 20-21)
structure.body: All things are clean, yet it is evil to build a stumbling block with your eating; love will gladly leave meat and wine on the table rather than trip a brother.

structure.label: Faith, Conscience, and the Closing Principle (v. 22-23)
structure.body: Hold your convictions before God; blessed is the man with no self-accusation. He who doubts is self-condemned when he acts — and whatever is not of faith is sin.

structure.label: Doxology: To Him Who Is Able to Establish You (v. 24-26)
structure.body: The letter's argument closes in worship: the God who is able to make your brother stand is able to establish you, publishing the once-hidden mystery for the obedience of faith among all the nations.

sections.heading: Who Were 'the Weak,' and Why This Fight Was Burning in Rome
paragraphs: Around AD 49 the emperor Claudius expelled the Jews from Rome — the decree that drove Priscilla and Aquila to Corinth, where Paul met them (Acts 18:2). For roughly five years the house churches of Rome were emptied of their Jewish believers and became thoroughly Gentile: Gentile leaders, Gentile customs, Gentile menus, Gentile calendars. Then Claudius died, the edict lapsed, and the Jewish believers came home — to congregations that no longer looked, ate, or kept time the way they had left them. Chapter 14 is Paul operating on that exact wound. He is not musing about vegetarianism; he is pastoring returning exiles and the people who filled their seats.

So who is 'weak in faith'? Not the lazy believer and not the immoral one. He is the man whose conscience is still bound where Christ has actually loosed him — typically a Jewish believer who could not buy meat in a city whose markets were fed by pagan sacrifice and whose butchers were no longer kosher, and who therefore did what Daniel did in Babylon and ate vegetables (Daniel 1:8-16). He kept Sabbaths and fast days because a thousand years of covenant faithfulness had trained him to. Read carefully: this man is often the more disciplined, more sacrificial, more scrupulous man in the room. Weakness of faith here is not weakness of devotion; it is faith that has not yet stretched to the size of its own freedom.

And Paul does take a side, which must be said plainly rather than blurred into false balance. Verse 14: 'nothing is unclean of itself.' Verse 20: 'All things indeed are clean.' Chapter 15:1 puts him squarely in one camp — 'Now we who are strong ought to bear the weaknesses of the weak, and not to please ourselves.' Paul is strong, he knows he is right, and he never once asks the weak brother to hurry up and get enlightened. He aims almost every command in the chapter at the person who is correct. That is the shock of Romans 14: being right is not the finish line. It is the starting position from which love is required to do something costly.

sections.heading: Two Sins at One Table — and What 'Don't Judge' Does Not Mean
paragraphs: Verse 3 names two different sins with two different words, and most of us are guilty of only one of them. The strong man 'despises' — exoutheneo, to reduce a person to nothing, the amused superiority of the enlightened. The weak man 'judges' — krino, to pass sentence, the cold satisfaction of the stricter man. Contempt and condemnation look nothing alike and do identical damage, because both are the same crime underneath: a man climbing onto a seat that is already occupied. Verse 10 puts them side by side and answers both with one picture — the bema of Christ.

But Romans 14 is not a blanket ban on discernment, and it must never be used as a shield for sin. The same apostle orders the Corinthian church to judge the man inside it and put him out (1 Corinthians 5:12-13). The same apostle withstood Peter to his face at Antioch over a table (Galatians 2:11-14) — and that is the crucial comparison. At Antioch the issue was whether Gentiles were full members of the covenant people by faith alone; that is the gospel, and Paul fought. In Rome the issue is meat and calendars, matters on which Scripture has bound no Christian conscience; that is opinion, and Paul refuses to legislate. Learn to tell the two apart, because most church wars are fought by people who have mistaken their preferences for the gospel and their gospel for a preference.

The modern list writes itself and Paul deliberately did not write it: alcohol, what you watch, what you listen to, how you keep Sunday, whether you mark Christmas, how you dress your family for church, schooling choices, medical choices, debt and money, political alignment, which translation you carry. The moment you turn Romans 14 into a ruling on those, you have missed it — because the chapter's rule is not a position on any of them. The rule is love (v. 15), and love takes a different concrete shape depending on who is sitting across the table from you.

sections.heading: 'Whatever Is Not of Faith Is Sin'
paragraphs: Verse 23 closes the chapter with a principle far bigger than dinner. Notice the mechanics: the man who doubts is condemned when he eats — and the food was clean the whole time. His sin was not the meat; his sin was acting while unpersuaded that God approved. Conscience is not the standard of truth (verse 14 has already ruled that nothing is unclean of itself), but conscience is binding on the man who holds it. Every time you override your own conviction of God's will, you are training yourself to move against God while calling it freedom, and that habit does not stay in the small things.

The cure is never to bulldoze a conscience — not your brother's and not your own. The cure is to educate it with the Word until faith honestly catches up, and to refuse to act ahead of it in the meantime. That is why verse 5 demands each man be 'fully assured in his own mind' and verse 22 blesses the man who does not condemn himself in what he permits. God is after a settled, instructed, unaccusing heart, not a compliant one.

And the principle expands past food to everything you do. Anything you cannot do in the confident persuasion that God is pleased with it — the purchase you argue yourself into, the relationship you keep quiet about, the habit you would drop the second a mature believer walked in, the thing you do while asking God in advance to overlook it — is sin for you, even if another believer could do it in perfect freedom. That is not legalism. Legalism binds everyone with one man's rules; this binds you with your own faith, before God, in private.

ntConnection.heading: New Testament Connection
paragraphs: The quotation at verse 11 is Isaiah 45:23, fused with the ancient oath formula 'as I live, says the LORD.' In Isaiah the context could not be more absolute: the LORD is declaring that He alone is God, that there is no other, and He swears by Himself that to Him every knee shall bow and every tongue shall swear allegiance. Now watch what Paul does with it in verse 10 — he cites the verse about bowing before the LORD to prove that 'we will all stand before the judgment seat of Christ.' (The manuscripts divide here: the tradition behind this translation reads 'the judgment seat of Christ,' while most modern critical editions read 'of God.' The argument is untouched either way — verse 12 says we give account to God, and Paul moves between the two without a flinch, because verse 9 has already established that Christ died and rose to be Lord of the dead and the living.) Paul makes the same move again in Philippians 2:10-11, where at the name of Jesus every knee bows and every tongue confesses that Jesus Christ is Lord. The highest Christology in the New Testament is deployed here to settle an argument about dinner — that is how seriously heaven takes the way you treat a brother.

Trace this chapter forward two ways. First, into 1 Corinthians 8-10, where Paul faces the identical question over meat sacrificed to idols and answers with the same logic in sharper form: 'Knowledge puffs up, but love builds up' (1 Corinthians 8:1) — there the verb oikodomeo, the same builder's word that stands behind the noun oikodome in verse 19 here — and he ends by saying he would give up meat forever rather than trip a brother (1 Corinthians 8:13). Second, into verse 14 itself. Paul says he is 'persuaded in the Lord Jesus' that nothing is unclean, and behind that stands the ruling of Jesus in Mark 7:14-23, where in declaring that nothing entering a man from outside can defile him, He made all foods clean — the same verdict God pressed on Peter three times on the rooftop in Joppa (Acts 10:9-16). Paul is not inventing a policy; he is enforcing his Lord's ruling. And the argument lands where the whole letter lands, in Romans 15:7 — 'Therefore accept one another, even as Christ also accepted you, to the glory of God.' The same verb as 14:1. Christ's welcome of you is the measure of your welcome of him.

lexicon.insight: Built from the negative particle and the word for strength — literally 'to be strengthless.' It is the same family of words used for the sick in the Gospels, and Paul's choice of it is deliberately gentle: a weak brother is not a rebel to be crushed but a patient to be carried. Note also where the weakness lies. He is not weak in obedience — he is often the most disciplined man at the table. He is weak in faith at one specific point: his grasp of his own liberty is not yet strong enough to bear the weight of it. You do not heal that with contempt or with pressure. Romans 15:1 gives the only prescription: 'we who are strong ought to bear the weaknesses of the weak.'

Literally to make a person out to be nothing — to treat him as zero, to write him off. This is the sin of the strong, and it almost never shows up as anger. It shows up as amusement: the raised eyebrow, the story told about him later, the private verdict that he is simply not where you are. It is the same word Luke uses for Herod and his soldiers setting Jesus at nothing before they mocked Him (Luke 23:11) — which tells you exactly how God classifies your smirk. You are not merely disagreeing with your brother. You are reducing to nothing a man for whom Christ died.

A courtroom word: to separate, distinguish, and then hand down a sentence. The chapter's hinge is verse 13, where Paul uses it twice in one breath and turns it around — 'let's not judge one another any more, but judge this rather.' He does not kill your capacity for judgment; he re-aims it. The verdicts you were spending on your brother's plate are to be spent on your own conduct. And do not miss verse 22's blessing on the man who does not judge himself in what he approves. Judgment turned outward destroys fellowship; judgment turned inward, before God, produces a clear conscience.

A proskomma is the thing your foot strikes — a stone or stump left in the path where a man walking at night will hit it and go down. Paul pairs it in verse 13 with skandalon (G4625), which is even sharper: the baited trigger-stick of a trap, the piece that springs the snare when it is touched. Put the two together and you have Paul's picture of a careless liberty — something you set down without malice that takes a brother's legs out from under him. And note what makes it a stumbling block: not the object, which is clean, but its placement. The same freedom is harmless in your own house and lethal in his road.

From the words for 'house' and 'to build' — architecture, construction, the raising of an actual structure. It is the positive command that the whole chapter has been driving at, and it is deliberately set against kataluo in verse 20, the word for demolishing a building stone by stone. So Paul hands you a builder's test for every disputed conversation: after I say this, will there be more of God's house standing, or less? Notice too that Paul says pursue — dioko, to chase down — the things that make for peace. Peace between believers is not what happens when nobody talks about it. It is hunted, on purpose, at cost.

holySpiritRevelation.intro: The Spirit is dealing with the contempt hidden inside your strength and the condemnation hidden inside your scruples — and with the fact that you have been sitting in a seat that belongs to Christ.

items.title: The Smirk and the Sentence
items.body: Two men sinned at that table in Rome, and only one of them thought he was the problem. If you are the free one, your sin will not feel like sin; it will feel like maturity. It is the amused sigh when someone won't watch that film, won't touch that drink, won't work on a Sunday — exoutheneo, quietly reducing a brother to nothing. If you are the strict one, your sin will feel like faithfulness. It is the settled verdict that people with your convictions love God more. So answer honestly: which of the two are you? Name the actual person whose walk with God you have been privately grading this month. And ask the question that exposes both sins at once — has your position on this matter made you kinder to that person, or only more certain about yourself?

items.title: Whose Servant Have You Been Managing?
items.body: 'Who are you who judge another's servant?' The Spirit is asking you for a name and an address. You have been standing in someone else's courtyard issuing orders about a man you do not own, do not feed, and cannot hold up. But hear the whole verse, because there is enormous relief in it: 'he will be made to stand, for God has power to make him stand.' The believer you are most anxious about — the one whose convictions you are sure will ruin him — is held by a hand stronger than his weakness and stronger than your worry. And so are you. You are not standing today because you got the disputed questions right; you are standing because God is able. So who have you been trying to hold up, or hold down, that God never handed to you? And can you actually take your hands off him and pray verse 4 over him instead?

items.title: Right — and Still Not Walking in Love
items.body: This is the sentence that ruins every argument you have ever won: 'if because of food your brother is grieved, you walk no longer in love.' Not 'you are mistaken.' Not 'you overstated it.' You have stepped off the road of love altogether, and Romans 13:10 has already told you that love is the fulfillment of the law — so you have stepped off the law of God while defending your rights under it. Then Paul weighs your liberty against something specific: the blood of Christ, spilled for the very brother it is costing. Here is the test, and it is not comfortable. The liberty you cannot lay down for a brother has stopped being a freedom and quietly become a master — because a free man can always put a thing down. What is the one thing you would fight to keep? Would you give it up for a person Jesus died for? And if the honest answer is no, which of you is actually the weak one?

audit.title: The Contempt Check
audit.body: Who in your life do you privately consider spiritually behind you? Say the word you use for them in your head — legalistic, extra, immature, still in bondage, compromised, worldly. Now put the verse next to that word: 'God has accepted him.' If God has already received the man you are quietly writing off, whose standard are you actually enforcing?

audit.title: The Bench Audit
audit.body: Make two short lists. First: the things you have judged people for in the last month that Scripture has nowhere actually commanded. Second: the things Scripture plainly commands that you have been dodging by saying 'don't judge me.' Romans 14 will not let you hide in either list. One of them is you on a seat that isn't yours; the other is you using Paul's mercy as a shield against Paul's Lord.

audit.title: The Doubt Line
audit.body: What are you doing right now that you cannot do with a settled conscience — the thing you argue yourself into, the thing you would put down instantly if a mature believer walked in, the thing you do while asking God in advance to overlook it? Verse 23 is blunt: that thing is sin for you, not because the thing is dirty, but because you did it without faith. Name it out loud, and stop pretending the doubt is a technicality.

practices.title: Laying One Thing Down, Silently
practices.body: Identify one genuine liberty of yours — a drink, a show, a joke, a habit, a spending pattern, a Sunday routine — that you know troubles one specific brother or sister. This week, in that person's presence, lay it down. Do not announce it, do not explain your sacrifice, do not let them thank you for it. Verse 22 says have your faith to yourself before God; let this cost land where only He sees it. Then keep it laid down for as long as you are near that person.

practices.title: The Builder's Three Questions
practices.body: Write these on a card and carry it this week: (1) Does this make for peace? (2) Does this build him up? (3) Whose servant is he? Ask all three before you speak into any disputed matter — in conversation, in a group chat, in a comment thread. And before Sunday, send one message to the person you have most despised or most judged, and receive them the way God received you: no correction attached, no argument reopened, just welcome. Then pray verse 4 over them by name — 'Lord, he is Your servant, and You are able to make him stand.'

prayerReflection: "Lord Jesus, You died, and rose, and lived again to be Lord of the dead and the living — and that means You are Lord of my brother, and Lord of me. Forgive me for the seat I have been sitting in. I have despised believers You have accepted; I have handed down sentences on a servant who does not answer to me; I have kept a file on people whose account will never be read to me. Take it out of my hands. Thank You that he will be made to stand — not because his convictions are perfect, but because You have the power to hold him up — and thank You that I am standing this morning for exactly the same reason. Search me now: is there anything of mine lying in a brother's road? Any stone I set down without thinking, any liberty I have carried into a place it wounds him? I would rather lay it down than grieve a man You bled for. Keep me walking in love, because the moment I stop, being right cannot save me. Let Your Kingdom be my measure — not eating and drinking, but righteousness, and peace, and joy in the Holy Spirit. Make me a builder and never a wrecker of Your work. And where I am uncertain, hold me back: whatever is not of faith is sin, so settle my heart in Your Word until I am fully assured in my own mind, and let me act only out of faith. To You, the only wise God, who is able to establish me — be the glory forever. In Jesus' name, Amen."

storyConnections.title: Daniel's Vegetables in a Pagan Palace
storyConnections.summary: Carried off to Babylon as a youth and enrolled in the king's own academy, Daniel 'purposed in his heart that he would not defile himself' with the royal food, and asked instead for vegetables and water. Scripture never states his reason — a Babylonian king's table would have broken the law's food rules, and its meat would have carried the shadow of the king's gods — but the line he drew was at his plate. God honored the scruple: after ten days he and his friends looked healthier than the boys eating the royal ration. Now put that man in a Roman house church six centuries later and read verse 2 again: 'he who is weak eats only vegetables.' The brother with the bowl of greens is not a coward or a legalist; he is a man with a Daniel-shaped conscience in a pagan city, guarding his loyalty to God the only way he knows how. Before you set him at nothing, remember whose company he is keeping.

storyConnections.title: The Rooftop Sheet and the Table at Antioch
storyConnections.summary: On a roof in Joppa, Peter saw heaven open and a sheet come down full of creatures he had refused to eat his entire life, and three times a voice told him not to call unclean what God had cleansed. That is the ruling standing behind Romans 14:14. And yet years later, at Antioch, the same Peter ate freely with Gentile believers until men came from James — and then he withdrew, and the rest of the Jewish believers followed him, and even Barnabas was carried away. Paul opposed him to his face, publicly. Learn the difference the two stories teach: when the question is a disputed opinion, Paul says receive one another and lay your liberty down; when the question is whether Gentiles are full members of God's people by faith alone, that is the gospel, and Paul fights. Wisdom is knowing which table you are sitting at.

storyConnections.title: Jerusalem's Letter to the Gentiles
storyConnections.summary: When the church council met in Jerusalem, James refused to 'trouble' the Gentiles turning to God with the yoke of the law — salvation was by grace, full stop. But the letter they sent asked the Gentile believers to abstain from meat sacrificed to idols, from blood, from things strangled, and from sexual immorality, so that Jew and Gentile could share one table without agony. Three of those four are food. That is Romans 14 in action years before Romans was written: the free were asked to limit their freedom, not because the food was dirty, but because a brother was worth more than a meal. The council did not solve the tension by declaring a winner. It solved it by asking love to move first — which is exactly what Paul asks of the strong in Rome, and of you.
